"'''Da Ya Think I'm Sexy?'''", also written "'''Da' Ya' Think I'm Sexy'''", is a song by British singer [[Rod Stewart]] from his ninth studio album, ''[[Blondes Have More Fun]]'' (1978). It was written by Stewart, [[Carmine Appice]], and Duane Hitchings,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.yamaha.com/allaccess/artists/issue10-hitchings_duane.asp?issue=issue10 |title=Duane Hitchings – A Country Writer's Rock Roots |access-date=14 January 2013 |publisher=Yamaha All Access}}</ref> though it incorporates the melody from the song "Taj Mahal" by [[Jorge Ben Jor]] and the string arrangement from the song "(If You Want My Love) Put Something Down On It" by [[Bobby Womack]].<ref name="autobiography">{{Cite book |last=Stewart |first=Rod |url=https://archive.org/details/rodautobiography0000stew/page/225 |title=Rod: The Autobiography |date=2012 |publisher=New York [N.Y.] : Crown Archetype |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-307-98730-3}}</ref>

The song was released as the first single from ''Blondes Have More Fun'' in November 1978. It spent one week atop the [[UK Singles Chart]] in December 1978 and four weeks atop the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] in February 1979. ''Billboard'' ranked it number four on its Top Singles of 1979 year-end chart.<ref>"Top Singles of the Year" ''Billboard'' 22 December 1979: TIA-10</ref> It also topped the charts in Canada for four weeks and in Australia for two weeks.

Royalties from the song were donated to the United Nations Children's Fund ([[UNICEF]]) and Stewart performed the song at the [[Music for UNICEF Concert]] at the [[United Nations General Assembly]] in January 1979.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Robesonian - Google News Archive Search |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ZDVVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=1z0NAAAAIBAJ&pg=5242,4080400 |access-date=9 April 2025 |website=news.google.com}}</ref>

"Da Ya Think I'm Sexy?", also written "Da' Ya' Think I'm Sexy", is a song by British singer Rod Stewart from his ninth studio album, Blondes Have More Fun (1978). It was written by Stewart, Carmine Appice, and Duane Hitchings, though it incorporates the melody from the song "Taj Mahal" by Jorge Ben Jor and the string arrangement from the song "(If You Want My Love) Put Something Down On It" by Bobby Womack.

The song was released as the first single from Blondes Have More Fun in November 1978. It spent one week atop the UK Singles Chart in December 1978 and four weeks atop the US Billboard Hot 100 in February 1979. Billboard ranked it number four on its Top Singles of 1979 year-end chart. It also topped the charts in Canada for four weeks and in Australia for two weeks.

Royalties from the song were donated to the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) and Stewart performed the song at the Music for UNICEF Concert at the United Nations General Assembly in January 1979.

sections.heading: Background and writing
sections.wikitext:
[[Carmine Appice]], who played drums on this song, told Songfacts: "This was a story of a guy meeting a chick in a club. At that time, that was a cool saying. If you listen to the lyrics, 'She sits alone, waiting for suggestions, he's so nervous...' it's the feelings of what was going on in a dance club. The guy sees a chick he digs, she's nervous and he's nervous and she's alone and doesn't know what's going on, then they end up at his place having sex, and then she's gone."<ref name="songfacts">{{Cite web | url = http://www.songfacts.com/detail.php?id=1306  | title = Da Ya Think I'm Sexy? | work = Songfacts.com  | access-date = 8 May 2009}}</ref> In a 2007 interview, co-writer Duane Hitchings noted that "Da Ya Think I'm Sexy?" was "a spoof on guys from the 'cocaine lounge lizards' of the ''[[Saturday Night Fever]]'' days. We Rock and Roll guys thought we were dead meat when that movie and the [[Bee Gees]] came out. The Bee Gees were brilliant musicians and really nice people. No big egos. Rod, in his brilliance, decided to do a spoof on disco. VERY smart man. There is no such thing as a 'dumb' super success in the music business."<ref>{{cite web |website= RockUnited.com |date=23 March 2007 |title=Duane Hitchings, The Man Behind the Hits |author= Urban "Wally" Wallstrom |access-date= 18 January 2013 |url= http://www.rockunited.com/hitchings.htm}}</ref>

After [[Rod Stewart]] rejected the original arrangement for the song, Appice instead used it for "I Just Fell in Love Again" on [[Carmen Maki]]'s 1979 album ''Night Stalker'', which he was working on at the same time.<ref>{{cite AV media |people=[[Carmine Appice|Appice, Carmine]] |date=29 April 2022|title=Carmine Appice recalls Carmen Maki's Night Stalker album 1979 カルメン・マキ|medium=video|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tnkTrA-7YmY|access-date=18 February 2024|publisher=Australian Rock Show|via=[[YouTube]]}}</ref>

Guitarist [[Jim Cregan]] attributed the song's success to the [[bass guitar]] line played by [[Phil Chen]], saying "That particular bass pattern, when he played that, the whole song seemed to fall into place. I was doing my [[Nile Rodgers]] impersonations."<ref name=egan/>

Carmine Appice, who played drums on this song, told Songfacts: "This was a story of a guy meeting a chick in a club. At that time, that was a cool saying. If you listen to the lyrics, 'She sits alone, waiting for suggestions, he's so nervous...' it's the feelings of what was going on in a dance club. The guy sees a chick he digs, she's nervous and he's nervous and she's alone and doesn't know what's going on, then they end up at his place having sex, and then she's gone." In a 2007 interview, co-writer Duane Hitchings noted that "Da Ya Think I'm Sexy?" was "a spoof on guys from the 'cocaine lounge lizards' of the Saturday Night Fever days. We Rock and Roll guys thought we were dead meat when that movie and the Bee Gees came out. The Bee Gees were brilliant musicians and really nice people. No big egos. Rod, in his brilliance, decided to do a spoof on disco. VERY smart man. There is no such thing as a 'dumb' super success in the music business."

After Rod Stewart rejected the original arrangement for the song, Appice instead used it for "I Just Fell in Love Again" on Carmen Maki's 1979 album Night Stalker, which he was working on at the same time.

Guitarist Jim Cregan attributed the song's success to the bass guitar line played by Phil Chen, saying "That particular bass pattern, when he played that, the whole song seemed to fall into place. I was doing my Nile Rodgers impersonations."

sections.heading: Music and lyrics
sections.wikitext:
Stewart biographer Sean Egan said of the music that "Stewart and his crew expertly purvey disco's [[four-on-the-floor]] drumbeat, clipped guitar approach, and throbbing bass style", adding that the song also contains a "soaring [[synthesizer|synth]] [[riff (music)|riff]] and a howling sax line."<ref name=egan/> 

Egan noted "a strange disconnect between choruses and verses."<ref name=egan/>  Egan described the choruses as "vainglorious, juvenile, icky and concerned with physical pleasure" but described the verses as being "unshowy and moving, revolving around a couple's mutual quest to find an intimacy deeper than sex in the heart of the pitiless, big city."<ref name=egan/>

Stewart biographer Sean Egan said of the music that "Stewart and his crew expertly purvey disco's four-on-the-floor drumbeat, clipped guitar approach, and throbbing bass style", adding that the song also contains a "soaring synth riff and a howling sax line." 

Egan noted "a strange disconnect between choruses and verses."  Egan described the choruses as "vainglorious, juvenile, icky and concerned with physical pleasure" but described the verses as being "unshowy and moving, revolving around a couple's mutual quest to find an intimacy deeper than sex in the heart of the pitiless, big city."

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext:
The song was criticised by many in the rock press as a betrayal of Stewart's [[Blues rock|blues-oriented rock]] roots, due to its [[disco]]-like arrangement, but Stewart and others were quick to point out that other widely respected artists, such as [[Paul McCartney]] and [[the Rolling Stones]], had also released disco-flavoured songs. However, the song has since experienced some retrospective acclaim as ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' placed the song at number 301 in its 2004 list of the [[500 Greatest Songs of All Time]].<ref name="500 Greatest Songs of All Time">{{cite news|title=500 Greatest Songs of All Time|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/500-greatest-songs-of-all-time-151127/rod-stewart-da-ya-think-im-sexy-47959/|newspaper=Rolling Stone|date=11 December 2003 |access-date=11 July 2022|author=Rolling Stone }}</ref>

''[[Cash Box]]'' said it has "a clipping bass line [by [[Phil Chen]]], steady kick drum and soaring synthesized strings", as well as "alternately gentle and dashing [[rhythm guitar]] work and a commanding [[saxophone|sax]] solo".<ref name=cb>{{cite news|title=CashBox Singles Reviews|date=16 December 1978|page=20|newspaper=Cash Box|accessdate=1 January 2022|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/70s/1978/CB-1978-12-16.pdf}}</ref>

In 1979, [[Tiny Tim (musician)|Tiny Tim]] performed "Do Ya Think I'm Sexy" on several television shows, including his final appearance on ''[[The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson]]''. During the performance, Tiny removed his jacket and dress shirt, which he tossed "to the cheering audience" before lifting his T-shirt, "bouncing wildly on his knees", and writhing on the stage for effect. Afterwards, [[Johnny Carson]] remarked, "There's just nothing that can be said."<ref>{{cite book | last=Martell | first=Justin |last2=Wray McDonald|first2=Alanna | title=Eternal Troubadour: The Improbable Life Of Tiny Tim | publisher=Jawbone Press | year=2016 |pages=334-335 | isbn=978-1-908279-87-3}}</ref>

In 1982, Tiny recorded a version of the song "in the style of [[Al Jolson]]". Gary Lawrence produced the song and released it as a single on his record label, Vo-Do-De-O-Do. Tim also appeared in a music video for the song, which aired on public-access television in Florida. Lawrence later stated, "The truth of the matter was basically Neil Hollander and Banner Talent were supposed to market the record and get me a deal with a label that would put it out and they actually dropped the ball on the whole thing".<ref name="Tim Single">{{cite book | last=Martell | first=Justin |last2=Wray McDonald|first2=Alanna | title=Eternal Troubadour: The Improbable Life Of Tiny Tim | publisher=Jawbone Press | year=2016 |pages=344-346 | isbn=978-1-908279-87-3}}</ref>

In 1997, the song was [[remix]]ed by British [[electronic dance music]] group [[N-Trance]] for their second album, ''[[Happy Hour (N-Trance album)|Happy Hour]]'' (1998), and features lyrics from the [[Millie Jackson]] version (as performed by vocalist [[Kelly Llorenna]]). It was featured in the film ''[[A Night at the Roxbury]]'' the following year. This version became a hit in late 1997, topping both the [[Recorded Music NZ|New Zealand Singles Chart]] for three weeks and the Czech Republic singles chart.<ref name="musicweek">{{cite magazine|first=|last=|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1997/Music-Week-1997-11-15.pdf|title=Artist Profile: N-Trance|magazine=[[Music Week]]|date=15 November 1997|page=18|accessdate=20 September 2022}}</ref> Additionally, the song peaked at number seven on the [[UK Singles Chart]] and earning a double-platinum sales certification in Australia, where it peaked at number three on the [[ARIA Singles Chart]].

In 1997, the song was remixed by British electronic dance music group N-Trance for their second album, Happy Hour (1998), and features lyrics from the Millie Jackson version (as performed by vocalist Kelly Llorenna). It was featured in the film A Night at the Roxbury the following year. This version became a hit in late 1997, topping both the New Zealand Singles Chart for three weeks and the Czech Republic singles chart. Additionally, the song peaked at number seven on the UK Singles Chart and earning a double-platinum sales certification in Australia, where it peaked at number three on the ARIA Singles Chart.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext: [[Larry Flick]] from ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' described the song as "another slice of flashback fever". He noted that "with its recognizable hook, booty-shakin' baseline, guest rap by [[Ricardo da Force]], diva wailings by Kelly Llorenna, and Stewart himself, this updated remake could very well become the surprise radio hit of the summer. Of course, it could also become this month's novelty record."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Larry|last=Flick|url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/90s/1999/BB-1999-05-08.pdf|title=Single Reviews|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=8 May 1999|access-date=10 February 2020|page=19|author-link=Larry Flick}}</ref> British magazine ''[[Music Week]]'' rated N-Trance's version four out of five in their review.<ref>{{cite magazine|first=|last=|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1997/Music-Week-1997-09-27.pdf|title=Reviews: Singles|magazine=[[Music Week]]|date=27 September 1997|page=33|accessdate=13 September 2022}}</ref>
